## Introduction
<!-- Would it be natural to mention the functional paper findings here, as a "we observed this, hence we want to explore the molecular data"?-->
Skeletal muscle mass and strength decline with age, a process that advances from approximately 50 years of age, accelerates after 70 and, if left unchecked, may progress to sarcopenia [@fragala_resistance_2019; @timmons_molecular_2016]. Low muscle mass and strength are associated with disease, disability and early all-cause mortality, and regular resistance training (RT) is the most effective strategy to prevent or counteract this decline [@fragala_resistance_2019; @li_associations_2018; @scheerman_sarcopenia_2021]. Older adults are expected to gain similar benefits from RT as the young [@chen_is_2023; @marzuca-nassr_muscle_2024], provided the anabolic stimulus is sufficient [@chen_is_2023; @marzuca-nassr_muscle_2024; @paulussen_anabolic_2021], of which training volume is a principal determinant [@schoenfeld_dose-response_2017].  

Whether the anabolic stimulus is sufficient may in part depend on how responsive aging skeletal muscle is to it. Earlier findings suggest that older adults have a less responsive skeletal muscle mass compared to young, with a lower muscle protein synthesis (MPS) response to a single session of RT or protein ingestion [@atherton_muscle_2012; @timmons_molecular_2016; @wall_aging_2015]. However, baseline levels of MPS do not differ by age, and the activity in MPS-influencing proteins (e.g. mTOR) is elevated in fasted muscle from older adults compared to the young [@hodson_molecular_2019; @timmons_molecular_2016; @markofski_effect_2015]. The increased baseline mTOR activity could represent a compensation to increased relative muscle loading due to age-related loss of muscle mass, or dysregulation of the mTOR complex [@timmons_molecular_2016]. Further, likely as a consequence of altered mTOR regulation, ribosomal gene transcription and ribosome biogenesis is reduced in older adults [@chaillou_does_2023; @hodson_molecular_2019; @timmons_molecular_2016]. The increase in ribosomal content following onset of RT is believed to provide support for skeletal muscle fibre hypertrophy, through increased translational capacity yielding a higher baseline MPS [@figueiredo_regulation_2019; @figueiredo_revisiting_2019]. Indeed, regardless of age, individuals who respond to RT exhibit an accumulation in markers of ribosome biogenesis (e.g., total RNA and/or rRNA), compared to those who do not experience benefits of RT [@hammarstrom_benefits_2020; @stec_ribosome_2016; @stec_effects_2015]. 

Given the dose-response relationship between training volume and gains in muscle mass and strength observed in younger adults [@schoenfeld_dose-response_2017], and recent findings that older "non-responders" can achieve improved hypertrophy with higher training volume [@lixandrao_higher_2024], increasing training volume may represent a strategy to enhance the anabolic stimulus and thereby support the ribosome biogenesis response necessary for adaptation. Therefore, the present study aimed to determine whether markers of ribosome biogenesis (total RNA, UBF, c-Myc) and the transcriptome respond differently to low- and moderate-volume RT in young and older adults.

### Study Overview

This study was conducted as an age-stratified within-participant trial employing a unilateral design. All participants performed a whole-body unilateral training program, with low- and moderate-volume protocols randomly assigned to either leg/arm. The intervention lasted 12 weeks, comprising 10 weeks of training and two weeks of testing (@fig-study-design). Participants completed 24 training sessions: two per week for the first five weeks, three per week for the following four weeks, and a taper to two sessions in the tenth and final week. Muscle biopsies were sampled at baseline, after three weeks of training (six sessions) and post-intervention. Effects of the intervention on muscle mass, strength and glucose tolerance are reported separately [@COMPANION]. Biopsies were sampled at the same time of day (± 2 h) in an overnight fasted state. Participants were asked to maintain their habitual physical activity level throughout the intervention and not to perform any additional heavy exercise. All participants gave their written informed consent before study enrollment. The study was approved by the Regional Committee for Medical and Health Research Ethics - South-East Norway (ID nr. 255224), pre-registered at clinicaltrials.gov (Identifier: NCT05063279), and conducted according to the Helsinki Declaration. 


### Participants

Thirty-two young (24 ± 3.1 years) and 49 old (75.5 ± 5.6 years) adults were recruited locally; 10 of the old participants were randomly allocated to a control group. Inclusion criteria were age 20–30 or above 70 years (Figure 1). Exclusion criteria were: insufficient Norwegian proficiency; RT more than once weekly and/or endurance training three or more times weekly within the last six months; unstable cardiovascular disease; illness or injury contraindicating RT; serious mental illness; or allergy to local anaesthesia.


### Resistance training protocol

Resistance training was performed as a whole-body training program. Each RT-session contained three lower-body exercises (unilateral leg press, unilateral knee extension and -flexion) and three upper-body exercises (unilateral chest-press, unilateral bent-over rows, and unilateral bicep curls), using individualized settings in all exercise apparatuses. The low training volume condition was performed as a single set of 10RM per exercise, and the moderate training volume condition was performed as three sets of 10RM per exercise. As a general warm-up, the participants cycled on an indoor exercise bicycle for 5-10 minutes. Before lower-body exercises the participants performed 1 set of 10 repetitions in bilateral leg press, and before upper-body exercises they performed a warm-up set of 10 push-ups, modified to their individual fitness level (e.g., standard, from the knees, or against a wall). To ensure progressive loading and an adequate stimulation of the skeletal muscle, the exercise load was increased in the following set if the participants lifted more than 12 repetitions. Resting time between each set was two minutes. For safety and standardization purposes, all sessions were monitored by trained personnel. To ensure sufficient recovery, at least one day separated training days throughout the intervention.


### Skeletal muscle sampling and analyses

Muscle biopsies were collected from m. vastus lateralis. The biopsies were sampled under antiseptic and anaesthetised conditions (Lidokain 10 mg ml-1, Mylan Hospital AS, Oslo Norway), using the micro-biopsy technique with a 12-14 gauge needle (Universal Plus, Mermaid medical A/S, Stenløse, Denmark) operated with a spring loaded biopsy gun (Bard Magnum, Bard Norway A/S, Oslo, Norway). Samples were divided into aliquots for RNA and protein analyses. At week 3 and 12 measurements, there were 48 hours between the previous training session and biopsy sampling. 


### Protein extraction and western blotting

```{r}
library(dplyr)

# Participants and samples that entered a brms model.
# Age group and allocation are joined from reliefdata, so the function
# works regardless of how each model coded its groups (tx / tx_sex).
model_n <- function(fit,
                    id = "participant",
                    sample_vars = c("participant", "time", "leg")) {
  d <- fit$data |>
    mutate(participant = as.character(.data[[id]]))
  
  groups <- reliefdata::relief_participants |>
    mutate(participant = as.character(participant),
           age_grp = if_else(age < 40, "young", "old")) |>
    distinct(participant, age_grp, allocation)
  
  overall <- tibble(
    participants = n_distinct(d$participant),
    samples = nrow(distinct(d[, sample_vars])),
    rows = nrow(d)   # technical replicates for total RNA
  )
  
  by_group <- d |>
    left_join(groups, by = "participant") |>
    summarise(.by = c(age_grp, allocation),
              participants = n_distinct(participant),
              samples = nrow(distinct(pick(all_of(sample_vars))))) |>
    arrange(age_grp, allocation)
  
  list(overall = overall, by_group = by_group)
}

names(readRDS("fits/02-protein/mhi2.post.rds")$data)

n_rna  <- model_n(readRDS("fits/01-total-rna/m4.post.rds"))
n_ubf  <- model_n(readRDS("fits/02-protein/mu2.post.rds"))
n_cmyc <- model_n(readRDS("fits/02-protein/mhi2.post.rds"))


```


The wet muscle tissue from `r n_ubf$overall$samples` samples was freeze-dried for 24h and dissected, then homogenised with a plastic rod in an ice cold lysis buffer. Briefly, 150ul of RIPA buffer was added per mg muscle tissue dry weight, with 1ul protease/phosphatase inhibitors per 100ul lysis buffer. The samples were kept on ice at all times except for when manually disrupting to homogenise the tissue, and then incubated for 30 min on a rotator while on ice. Following the incubation, the samples were spun in the centrifuge for 40 min, at 15 000g at 4°C. Total protein was then diluted to 2ug/ul stock and aliquoted to run the samples in triplicates for protein concentration determination and for western blotting. Protein concentration was determined in a 1:10 dilution (Pierce Detergent Compatible Bradford Assay Reagent, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Oslo, Norway).

Western blots were done using the Jess Automated Western Blot System (Bio-Techne, Minneapolis, USA), according to the manufacturer's protocol, optimized for our lab. The stock solution (2ug/ul) was prepared with fluorescent master mix from the EZ standard pack (Bio-Techne) and 0.1X sample buffer (Bio-Techne) and thus diluted to 0.75 ug/ul for the assay. The assay samples were then briefly vortexed, denatured at 95°C, vortexed and spun down prior to loading the assay plate. To control for within-plate variation, we used a total protein normalization reagent (Bio-Techne) for all assays. A specific between-plate normalization was not used, however, all samples from one participant were analyzed on the same plate. Primary antibodies were purchased from Santa Cruz Biotechnology (Texas, USA): UBF 1:50, UBF F-9, sc-13125; and Cell Signaling Technology (Massachusetts, USA): c-Myc 1:15, c-Myc D84C12. Ready-to-use secondary antibodies (anti-mouse and anti-rabbit) were purchased from Bio-Techne. After loading, the assay plate was centrifuged at 2500 rpm for 5 min at room temperature. The assay was then run on the Jess system, with the chemiluminescence detection module.

### Total RNA extraction and RNA sequencing

Total RNA was extracted from `r n_rna$overall$samples` samples of muscle tissue, homogenised using TRIzol, 0.5mm RNase-free Zirconium beads (\~50 ul; Next Advanced, Averill Park, NY, USA) and mechanical agitation (Bullet Blender, Next Advanced, Averill Park, NY, USA). Chloroform (Sigma-Aldrich, Oslo, Norway) was used for phase separation, and the RNA pellet was precipitated with isopropanol (VWR International, Oslo, Norway). For assessment of RNA content and purity, RNA was eluted in TE buffer (1:2) and assessed via spectrophotometry. Samples with a 260/280 ratio below 1.8 were excluded. The RNA stock was stored at -80°C until further analyses.

`r nsamp` total RNA samples were selected for RNA-sequencing analysis of which `r nsamp_included` samples passed initial quality assessment (RIN > 8) and were used in downstream analyses. The samples were selected from the pool of intervention participants that had both baseline and post samples collected. Purified mRNA (poly-T oligo-attached magnetic beads) was used for library preparation and subsequent 150-bp paired-end sequencing (Illumina NovaSeq, Novogene Europe, Cambridge, United Kingdom). Raw reads were filtered (SOFTWARE, settings) and aligned to the Human genome (Release) followed by gene and transcript level quantification using RSEM (version).

Gene counts (filtered for low-abundance targets) were modeled using a regularized negative binomial generalized linear mixed model [@glmmmtb] including model parameters for sex, time (baseline and post-intervention), age-group (young and old) and condition (low- and moderate-volume) and the interaction between time age and condition. A varying intercept (random effect) was used for participant, and the dispersion parameter was estimated using the `nbinom2` parameterization available in `glmmTMB`[@glmmmtb]. The effective library size [@robinson2010;@edger] was included as an offset to account for sequencing depth. Regularization through an empirical Bayes shrinkage approach[@efron2010] was achieved using a two-step approach. First, naive models were fitted for all target counts (gene/transcript) using our in-house pipeline [@seqwrap] and estimates for all model parameters (except the intercept) were used to create priors for subsequent informed models. Fixed effect priors were constructed using a normal distribution with mean and standard deviations from each parameter value from the first model pass, the prior for the varying intercepts were constructed using a gamma distribution with the shape parameter informed by the mean from the naive model estimates and the  scale parameter fixed to 2. Finally, the dispersion parameter priors were constructed by fitting a trend model (Local Polynomial Regression Fit) to the association between raw mean log counts and log dispersion across all targets. The predicted dispersion at target-specific raw mean log count was used as the mean and the model residual standard error was used as the standard deviation to define a normally distributed target-specific prior.


### Statistical analyses

Total RNA yield was analysed with a Bayesian multilevel regression (brms) on the log scale, with treatment group, time and their interaction, adjusted for log tissue mass. Varying intercepts were included for participant, leg and sample, and a participant-specific time slope was included. The model was fitted to the individual spectrophotometer readings, so that technical replicate variance was separated from biological variance. Protein abundance (UBF and c-Myc, high peak) was analysed with Bayesian multilevel regression on the log scale, with group-by-sex-by-time cell means and varying intercepts for participant and leg. The primary protein outcome was the peak area normalised to total protein. Contrasts were computed from the posterior draws, and the protein contrasts weighted sexes equally. Results are reported as percentage changes or ratios of changes (posterior mean, 95% credible interval). P(>0) or P(<0), in the direction of the estimate, is given when the interval includes zero. Evidence was classified as credible (95% interval excludes zero), likely (≥ 90%), weak (75–90%) or no evidence (< 75%). Protein sensitivity analyses used the area without normalisation, exclusion of capillaries with a low normalisation factor or a Compass warning, and a plate intercept. Gene-level RNA-seq counts (16,878 genes after expression filtering) were analysed with negative-binomial mixed models (glmmTMB) containing sex, age group, and a combined time-by-volume term, with their interaction with age group, a participant-level varying intercept, and the TMM-normalised library size as an offset. Model parameters were regularised with empirical Bayes priors derived from a first, uninformed pass. Contrasts were computed from the model predictions with sexes weighted equally and tested with Wald tests. P-values were adjusted within each contrast (Benjamini–Hochberg, FDR < 5%), and rank-based gene-set enrichment analysis (Gene Ontology biological processes) was run on the contrast statistics.

### Exercise Volume Load

Total volume load was about 2.8 times higher with moderate than with low volume in both age groups (young: 137,439 ± 54,492 vs. 50,694 ± 25,708 kg; old: 118,125 ± 38,225 vs. 42,134 ± 14,353 kg).

### Protein

_UBF_
Older adults in the intervention group (averaged across volume conditions) tended to increase UBF protein content by week 3 (@fig-protein-rna A, 20.4%, 95% CI [−5.6%, 50.4%], P(>0) = 93.3%), as did the control group (27.6%, 95% CI [−4.2%, 64.8%], P(>0) = 95.2%), with no evidence of a difference between them (−3.9%, 95% CI [−33.2%, 35.9%], P(<0) = 63.1%). Young adults (averaged across volume conditions) also tended to increase UBF (16.9%, 95% CI [−7.1%, 45.2%], P(>0) = 91.0%), with no evidence of a difference from older adults (−1.4%, 95% CI [−29.7%, 33.9%], P(<0) = 57.0%). Within young adults, there was weak evidence of an increase with both low-volume (17.1%, 95% CI [−14.4%, 55.1%], P(>0) = 83.2%) and moderate-volume training (18.2%, 95% CI [−15.8%, 60.2%], P(>0) = 82.6%), with no evidence of a difference between them (3.4%, 95% CI [−34.7%, 56.9%], P(>0) = 51.1%). In older adults, low-volume training tended to increase UBF (29.8%, 95% CI [−8.4%, 77.3%], P(>0) = 92.0%), whereas there was no evidence of a change with moderate-volume training (13.2%, 95% CI [−19.0%, 57.1%], P(>0) = 74.6%), and no evidence of a difference between them (−10.1%, 95% CI [−44.9%, 41.5%], P(<0) = 71.6%). There was no evidence that the volume effect differed between age groups (21.9%, 95% CI [−41.3%, 117.3%], P(>0) = 67.9%).

_c-Myc High Peak_
c-Myc (high peak, @fig-protein-rna B) decreased in the control group by week 3 (−35.8%, 95% CI [−55.4%, −11.2%]). Older adults in the intervention group (averaged across volume conditions) tended to increase c-Myc (26.0%, 95% CI [−6.7%, 65.7%], P(>0) = 93.5%), and their change was greater than that of the control group (102.9%, 95% CI [22.4%, 211.1%]), a difference driven by the decrease in the control group. Young adults (averaged across volume conditions) showed weak evidence of an increase (19.8%, 95% CI [−9.1%, 54.3%], P(>0) = 89.5%), with no evidence of a difference from older adults (−2.9%, 95% CI [−34.8%, 41.5%], P(<0) = 60.1%). Within young adults, there was no evidence of a change with low-volume training (4.4%, 95% CI [−28.5%, 48.4%], P(>0) = 54.9%), whereas moderate-volume training tended to increase c-Myc (40.4%, 95% CI [−9.1%, 106.1%], P(>0) = 93.5%), with weak evidence of a difference between them (39.6%, 95% CI [−24.4%, 134.6%], P(>0) = 85.2%). In older adults, there was no evidence of a change with low-volume training (10.8%, 95% CI [−28.8%, 62.4%], P(>0) = 65.5%), whereas moderate-volume training tended to increase c-Myc (46.6%, 95% CI [−5.8%, 116.2%], P(>0) = 95.6%), again with weak evidence of a difference between them (38.3%, 95% CI [−26.1%, 138.5%], P(>0) = 82.6%). There was no evidence that the volume effect differed between age groups (10.9%, 95% CI [−54.8%, 140.8%], P(>0) = 50.0%).

### Total RNA

Older adults in the intervention group (averaged across volume conditions) increased total RNA yield (@fig-protein-rna C) by 9.4% from baseline to week 3 (95% CI [0.7%, 18.6%]) and by 14.1% to post (95% CI [5.2%, 23.2%]). Young adults increased by 17.4% at week 3 (95% CI [7.8%, 28.0%]) and by 11.8% at post (95% CI [2.5%, 21.6%]). All four intervention groups increased by post, credibly for older low volume (12.5%, 95% CI [1.1%, 24.3%]), older moderate volume (15.9%, 95% CI [4.8%, 28.1%]) and young moderate volume (12.4%, 95% CI [0.5%, 25.9%]), and likely for young low volume (11.3%, 95% CI [−0.9%, 24.8%], P(>0) = 96.3%). The control group showed no change at week 3 (−0.8%, 95% CI [−15.4%, 15.2%], P(<0) = 55.6%) and likely increased by post (14.0%, 95% CI [−3.2%, 34.0%], P(>0) = 93.8%), a magnitude similar to the intervention groups. There was no evidence of a difference between older intervention and control adults at post (0.8%, 95% CI [−16.6%, 20.0%], P(>0) = 51.7%), and only weak evidence of a larger increase in the intervention groups at week 3 (11.0%, 95% CI [−7.2%, 31.7%], P(>0) = 87.0%). From week 3 to post, the control group likely increased (15.5%, 95% CI [−4.4%, 38.3%], P(>0) = 93.0%), and the change was weakly smaller in the older intervention groups than in control (−8.8%, 95% CI [−26.3%, 11.4%], P(<0) = 81.8%). Young adults showed weak evidence of a larger week-3 increase than older adults (7.4%, 95% CI [−4.4%, 20.8%], P(>0) = 88.3%) and likely a smaller change from week 3 to post (−8.5%, 95% CI [−20.2%, 5.3%], P(<0) = 90.2%). There was no evidence of an age difference in the total change by post (−1.9%, 95% CI [−12.3%, 9.8%], P(<0) = 64.3%). There was no evidence of a volume effect at any interval in young or older adults (moderate vs. low volume, all P in the direction of the estimate between 55.1% and 74.1%, e.g. older at post 3.3%, 95% CI [−9.4%, 17.7%], P(>0) = 67.2%), nor of an age difference in the volume effect (e.g. at post −1.5%, 95% CI [−19.6%, 19.6%], P(<0) = 57.9%).

_Baseline_
Comparing gene-expression profiles between age groups at baseline (Young − Old) revealed marked differences, with `r n_diff_expressed` genes showing robust differences between the groups (FDR < 5%, Fig. [-@fig-rnaseq-combined]A–B). Rank-based gene-set enrichment analysis [@xu2024a] indicated that young participants had relatively higher expression of genes related to aerobic energy metabolism (oxidative phosphorylation) and relatively lower expression of genes related to immune system activation (complement activation, classical pathway) and epigenetic regulation of gene expression (heterochromatin formation). Training induced a large, broad transcriptional response in both age groups: `r n_sig_young_t3` genes changed from baseline to post in young participants, and `r n_sig_old_t3` in old participants (FDR < 5%). Individual genes with the strongest training-induced changes were predominantly collagen and basement-membrane genes in both groups (e.g., COL4A1, COL4A2, LAMB1, PXDN in young; COL4A1, LAMA4, COL3A1, COL1A2, SPARC in old).

_Training-effect_
Rank-based gene-set enrichment analysis [@xu2024a] showed that the dominant biology of the training response was similar between age groups: 6 of the top 10 enriched categories were shared, with matching direction and comparable magnitude in both young and old (RNA splicing, ribonucleoprotein complex biogenesis, integrin-mediated signaling pathway, cell adhesion mediated by integrin, collagen metabolic process, and mRNA transport). Training up-regulated genes related to ECM/connective tissue remodeling (e.g., integrin-mediated signaling and adhesion, collagen metabolic process) and down-regulated genes related to RNA-processing and ribosome biogenesis (e.g., RNA splicing, ribonucleoprotein complex biogenesis, mRNA transport) in both groups. While essentially no genes (1 gene at 5% and 0 at 1%) showed a statistically significant age-dependent training response after FDR correction, gene-set enrichment analysis of the age × time interaction contrast revealed (Fig. [-@fig-rnaseq-combined]C–D) that the magnitude of the shared training response differed somewhat between age groups in specific processes: the down-regulation of RNA splicing and related mRNA-processing categories was more pronounced in young than old, while the up-regulation of angiogenesis and aerobic respiration/cellular respiration categories was more pronounced in young than old.

A smaller set of categories differed by age: young participants showed additional enrichment for cytoplasmic translation, mesenchymal cell migration, and angiogenesis, while old participants showed additional enrichment for coagulation- and vascular-related categories. In contrast to the broadly age-independent training effect, the effect of training volume (moderate vs. low) was age-dependent: a substantial number of genes differed by volume in old participants (`r n_sig_old_volume_t3` genes, FDR < 5%), while only one gene showed a volume effect in young participants. Among old participants, higher training volume was associated with relatively higher expression of genes related to mitochondrial biogenesis and oxidative metabolism (e.g., inner mitochondrial membrane organization, respiratory electron transport chain, purine-containing compound biosynthesis) and relatively lower expression of genes related to muscle contractile function and translation (e.g., skeletal muscle contraction, cytoplasmic translation, muscle organ development, striated muscle cell differentiation, ribosomal small subunit biogenesis). This volume effect was considerably more modest than the main training effect, both in the number of genes involved and in statistical strength. 


## Discussion

<!-- Opening -->
The main findings were that markers of ribosome biogenesis increased with training in both age groups, but on different timescales. Total RNA rose later in the old (post) than the young (week 3), with no clear difference between the age groups at post and no clear difference between low and moderate volume. UBF and c-Myc protein, measured at basline and week 3 only, tended to increase in the trained groups. However, UBF increased just as much in the old control group, whereas c-Myc decreased in control and rose with moderate-volume training in the trained groups. The RNA-sequencing data showed a large and largely age-independent training response, dominated by up-regulation of ECM and collagen genes and down-regulation of RNA-processing and ribosome-biogenesis related genes. A volume effect on the transcriptome was observed in the old only. 

<!-- Markers of ribosome biogenesis: old vs. young -->
The findings of the present study suggest that ribosome biogenesis is delayed rather than blunted in the old, as the old intervention group reached a similar change in total RNA as the young, only later. The young followed the expected early rise at week 3 (low = 15.7%, mod = 19.2%), as seen in previous data from our lab [@lian_glucose_2024; @hammarstrom_ribosome_2022; @hammarstrom_benefits_2020]. The old had started to accumulate total RNA at week 3 (low = 10.3%, mod = 8.3%), but with less certainty (93-97% probability of an increase). By post, the old had reached a similar level as the young (old: 12.3-15.8%, young: 10.8-12.2%), with a rising pattern in the old compared to a downward trend in the young. An elevation above baseline but a downward trend such as seen in the young in the present study is not surprising, as previous studies show the same pattern; an early rise after 2-3 weeks of RT onset, followed by a plateau or decline after several weeks of RT [@hammarstrom_benefits_2020; @hammarstrom_ribosome_2022; @brook_synchronous_2016]. More interesting is the continued rise in the old group from week 3 to post, effectively catching up to the young by post. While there was weak evidence for a greater increase in the young compared to the old at week 3, the difference between them was essentially down to a coin-toss at post. While total RNA thus accumulated at a slower rate in the old, there was no clear difference between the age groups, which does not support a blunted accumulation of total RNA. Acute rodent studies point the same way, although concentration rose later in the old in one of them [@haddad_aging-sensitive_2006; @west_normal_2019].

This contrasts the general findings of previous studies comparing old and young [@stec_effects_2015; @brook_synchronous_2016], or investigating old only [@stec_ribosome_2016; @lixandrao_molecular_2025], though these are far from clear-cut comparisons. Stec et al. [@stec_effects_2015] measured total RNA acutely in old and young, i.e., at baseline and 24 hours after a single session, and observed that old had a higher baselin total RNA (28%), but none of the groups changed 24 hours after the session. The study by Brook et al. [@brook_synchronous_2016] is likely the closest comparison, including old and young exercising unilaterally for six weeks. However, their biopsies were sampled about 90 min after RT, quite different from the 48 hours in the present study, and showed a 42% increase in the young after three weeks of RT and a trend at week six, while no change was observed in the old. Lixandrao et al. [@lixandrao_molecular_2025] included old only, exercising unilaterally for 10 weeks, with biopsies at baseline and 48 hours after the last session. They found a 7.5% non-significant increase, mostly in high and medium responders, roughly half of what was observed in the present study. In Stec et al. [@stec_ribosome_2016], 42 older adults exercised for four weeks (12 sessions), and total RNA was reported by responder cluster only, with a non-significant 9% increase in moderate responders and 26% in extreme responders. Timing of biopsy sampling could explain som of these differences, and so could the exercise programs, which differ in volume, frequency and duration. Stec et al. [@stec_ribosome_2016] used a whole-body program of two sets per exercise, three times a week. Brook et al. [@brook_synchronous_2016] used a unilateral knee-extension program (one trained leg, one untrained control leg) three times a week, and Lixandrao et al. [@lixandrao_molecular_2025] a unilateral knee-extension program (1-set vs. 4-set) two times a week for 10 weeks, with 20g of whey protein taken twice a day. The present study may have employed a heavier program than Brook et al. (2016) and Lixandrao et al. (2025), with six unilateral exercises overall (three upper-, three lower extremeties), which over time could have led to a higher accumulation in total RNA. This alone cannot explain the lack of a response in the old in Brook et al. (2016), however, since their young participants trained identically and did increase total RNA. The exercise program in Stec et al. (2016) was closer to the present one, and showed increases in total RNA in the responder clusters, adding to the notion that old may simply need a higher volume and/or more time exercising to accumulate total RNA. 

Notably, in the present study, the old control group showed a similar baseline-to-post increase in total RNA as the old intervention group (13.5%), though this was a weaker, less certain estimate than in the trained groups, and the difference between them was essentially zero at post. From baseline to week 3, the change in the control group was flat (-0.9%). Post strength testing was conducted three to four days prior to the biopsy, whereas there was no strength testing around the week 3 biopsy, but no evidence show that strength testing alone raises total RNA. Total RNA is also a variable measure [@godwin_relative_2024; @lundberg_early_2020], and prior biopsies have been reported to alter gene expression and tissue characteristics in later samples from the same muscle when taken hours to a week apart [@friedmann-bette_similar_2012; @van_thienen_biochemical_2014; @long_short-term_2023], although not in all studies [@lundby_gene_2005]. Whether this extends to biopsies taken weeks apart, as here, is not clear. As a result, the comparison between the old intervention and control group at post provides limited information on training effects, and the week 3 contrast between intervention and control is the cleaner comparison.

UBF and c-Myc protein, measured at baseline and week 3 only, followed the total RNA pattern in the trained groups. UBF tended to increase in all four intervention groups, albeit weakly (low volume: young 15.2%, old 27.1%; moderate volume: young 17.6%, old 13.1%), but also in the old control group (24.9%), which suggests a general temporal effect rather than a training-specific response. The c-Myc response was more training-specific: it fell in the old control group (-34.5%), and rose after moderate-volume training in both age groups (young 37.3%, old 47.9%), with no evidence of an age difference. Observed changes in the trained groups match previous short-term and acute findings [@figueiredo_impact_2016; @lian_glucose_2024], although a residual acute response cannot be excluded, since the week 3 biopsies were taken 48 hours after the last session and c-Myc and UBF protein have been found elevated 24-48 hours after a single session [@figueiredo_impact_2016]. Earlier human studies of older adults give a mixed picture. Stec et al. [@stec_effects_2015] found no change in UBF or c-Myc 24 hours after a single session in either age group, but noted that short-lived responses are missed at that time point. After the first session, Brook et al. [@brook_2016] found that c-Myc mRNA, c-Myc protein and TIF-1A rose in the young only, with biopsies taken about 90 minutes after the session, an acute window that the present study did not sample. Their response after the first session is therefore not directly comparable to a response after three weeks. After four weeks of training in older adults, c-Myc protein rose in all response clusters (+51% in non-responders, +250-357% in moderate and extreme responders), whereas UBF did not differ between clusters [@stec_ribosome_2016]. This is directionally consistent with the old intervention group in the present study, although without an untrained control group a time effect cannot be excluded, and the old control group here moved in the opposite direction for c-Myc. What does not quite add up is the increase of UBF in the control group paired with a decrease in c-Myc, since UBF is expected to be a downstream and training-specific target of c-Myc's transcriptional control [@figueiredo_impact_2016]. Total UBF protein has also been found to be a noisy measure, as in Figueiredo et al. [@figueiredo_ribosome_2015], where total UBF was unchanged after eight weeks while phosphorylated UBF (Ser388) rose fivefold at rest, so the UBF result should be interpreted with caution.

<!--Ribosome biogenesis markers: low vs. moderate volume-->
Training volume had little influence on total RNA in the present study. There was no evidence of a difference between low and moderate volume in the young (week 3: 2.9%; post: 1.1%) or in the old (week 3: -1.9%; post: 3.1%), and no evidence that the volume effect differed between age groups. This is in line with Lixandrao et al. [@lixandrao_2025], who found no volume effect (1 vs. 4 sets) on total RNA, c-Myc or UBF in older adults after 10 weeks, and with Hammarstrom et al. [@hammarstrom_ribosome_2022], who found no volume effect on total RNA in young. The latter should be interpreted with care, since both legs performed the same volume in the first four sessions, when most of the rise occurred. The closest comparison for the young is Hammarstrom et al. [@hammarstrom_benefits_2020], who found 8.8% higher total RNA with three compared to one set after four sessions (week 2), which had narrowed to 5.9%, with a confidence interval including zero, by week 12. The present study's week 3 estimate in the young (2.9%) is compatible with their 8.8%, so the data cannot rule out an early advantage of moderate volume that washes out later. Taken together with the previous studies, it seems that volume does not have a lasting influence on total RNA accumulation, at least not at the volumes compared here. c-Myc was the only marker with some indication of a volume effect. At week 3, moderate volume tended to increase c-Myc in both the young (37.3%) and the old (47.9%), whereas low volume did not (young 4.4%, old 9.6%), with weak evidence of a larger increase under moderate volume in both age groups (84-86% probability), and no evidence that this differed by age. The direction fits the higher c-Myc mRNA response to a moderate-volume session observed by Hammarstrom et al. [@hammarstrom_benefits_2020], although this was mRNA measured one hour after a session, and not resting protein. UBF showed no such pattern, with no evidence of a volume difference in either age group, and if anything a weak lean towards a larger increase with low volume in the old. The c-Myc result must be interpreted with caution, as the intervals were wide and the evidence weak, and since it was not accompanied by a difference in total RNA or UBF. The fact that low-volume training did not yield a meaningful c-Myc change in the old may nonetheless corroborate the notion that a higher volume is more important for the old [@lixandrao_higher_2024], though in the present study this was not specific to the old. A further complication is that ribosome-related transcripts do not necessarily keep increasing with training. Brown et al. [@brown_2024] found no increase in ribosome-related gene expression after 10 weeks of RT in young adults, and those with the largest gain in lean mass had the lowest baseline expression and the smallest change. They proposed that increases in translational capacity are acute and transient, followed by a refinement toward higher efficiency, which would make any volume effect on capacity markers hard to detect at later time points.

<!--Transcriptome: age and training response-->
The RNA-seq pattern observed in the present study closely matches previous findings. An earlier metformin trial in older adults found progressive resistance training to increase expression of genes involved in ECM remodelling and to down-regulate genes in RNA-processing pathways [@kulkarni_metformin_2020], the same two dominant, opposite-direction gene sets observed here. A recent reanalysis across training modalities in aged muscle likewise found that resistance training was mainly linked to ECM, collagen, adhesion and basement membrane genes, with negative enrichment of ribosome and spliceosome terms [@yang_transcriptomic_2026]. Notably, the present study adds a young comparison group, and shows that the training response was largely age-independent: 6 of the top 10 enriched categories were shared with matching direction and comparable magnitude, and essentially no individual genes showed an age-dependent response after FDR correction. Gene-set enrichment did suggest that the old had a smaller-magnitude version of the shared response, with less down-regulation of RNA splicing and less up-regulation of angiogenesis and aerobic respiration than the young. Whether this reflects the slower total RNA accumulation in the old is not possible to say from the present data, but it would fit the idea of a delayed rather than absent response.

The baseline differences between age groups were marked, with young showing relatively higher expression of oxidative phosphorylation genes, and relatively lower expression of immune-activation (complement) and heterochromatin-formation genes. Lower mitochondrial gene expression in old muscle is a consistent finding, both at the transcript level [@melov_resistance_2007] and the protein level [@deane_proteomic_2022], and Melov et al. [@melov_resistance_2007] additionally reported that 179 of 596 age-related genes shifted toward the young pattern after 26 weeks of resistance training. Kulkarni et al. [@kulkarni_metformin_2020] similarly found that a number of age-related differences in RNA-processing genes were no longer present after training. The present data do not directly show such convergence, since the age-by-training interaction was essentially null at the single-gene level, but the enrichment results point in the same direction as the shared training response, and a formal test of convergence would need a different analysis. Impaired transcriptional responses in mitochondrial, ECM and immune system genes have also been described as defining features of age-related anabolic resistance to resistance training [@deane_proteomic_2022], and the baseline differences here are in line with the first and the last of these. The training response in ECM genes, on the other hand, was clearly present in the old.

The down-regulation of RNA-processing and ribosome-biogenesis gene categories at post compared to baseline may at first glance seem inconsistent with the increased total RNA over the same period. Importantly, the RNA-seq data are of poly-A selected mRNA, so they say nothing directly about rRNA, which makes up the majority of total RNA [@haddad_aging-sensitive_2006; @stec_ribosome_2016], and the two readouts are therefore not contradictory. A similar dissociation has been seen in other studies, where the 45S pre-rRNA fell while total RNA rose after 6-12 weeks of RT [@mobley_biomarkers_2018; @haun_pre-training_2019], and Brown et al. [@brown_2024] found no increase, or a decrease, in ribosome-related transcripts across 10 weeks. Mobley et al. [@mobley_biomarkers_2018] proposed that this reflects negative feedback, once translational capacity has been built up, which is one possible reading of the present data. Because of the different molecules measured, however, this should be seen as an analogy rather than evidence, and an alternative is that the transcript changes reflect a shift in muscle fiber composition or in the relative proportion of non-muscle cells (e.g., through ECM remodelling), rather than a change within the muscle fibers.

<!--Transcriptome: training volume-->
In contrast to the broadly age-independent training effect, the effect of training volume on the transcriptome was age-dependent. A substantial number of genes differed between moderate and low volume in the old (1,216 genes, FDR < 5%), whereas essentially no genes did in the young. In the old, moderate volume was associated with relatively higher expression of mitochondrial biogenesis and oxidative metabolism genes, and relatively lower expression of muscle contractile and translation genes (e.g., cytoplasmic translation, RNA splicing, mRNA processing, ribosomal small subunit biogenesis). The effect was considerably more modest than the main training effect, both in the number of genes and in statistical strength. The lack of a volume effect in the young is in line with the molecular findings of Hammarstrom et al. [@hammarstrom_benefits_2020], where differences between volume conditions in rRNA were present early but had faded by the end of training, and the post biopsy in the present study may have been taken too late to capture the early differences.

The only comparable transcriptomic data in older adults are from Lixandrao et al. [@lixandrao_2025], who compared one and four sets of unilateral RT using RNA-seq in 9 older adults per responder group, and found no individual genes that differed between volume conditions. Using a latent-variable approach (PLIER), however, they found that medium responders had a lower immune, proteasome and spliceosome component with four sets than with one, which goes in the same direction as the lower RNA splicing and mRNA processing categories with moderate volume in our old participants. The number of participants in their analysis is far smaller than in the present study, which may explain why the gene-level result differed. An interesting feature of the present result is that the higher volume was associated with lower expression of translation-related genes at the same time as c-Myc tended to be higher at week 3 with moderate volume, and total RNA did not differ. One reading is that more volume brings forward the same decline in ribosome-related transcripts that was seen across both volume conditions, consistent with the refinement idea of Brown et al. [@brown_2024], but this is speculative. The higher expression of mitochondrial genes with moderate volume could reflect a shift in the training adaptation toward oxidative metabolism, and mitochondrial and ribosomal adaptations have been suggested to compete, although a review of the literature concluded that there is little evidence of such a trade-off [@mesquita_skeletal_2021]. Whether the volume effect in the old represents something meaningful for the functional outcomes, such as the greater hypertrophy with moderate volume, is not possible to say from the present data.

<!--Strengths, limitations and conclusion-->
A strength of the present study is the inclusion of both young and old participants, an untrained old control group, and a within-participant comparison of volume conditions, which removes between-participant variation as an explanation for any volume effect. Only one earlier human training study had, as of a recent review, compared ribosome biogenesis markers between young and old [@chaillou_does_2023], and we are not aware of studies combining this with a transcriptome-wide analysis and a volume manipulation. <!--[CHECK: novelty claim, needs a literature check before submission]--> Several limitations should be considered. First, the post-strength tests were poorly timed relative to the biopsies. Post testing was conducted three to four days before the biopsy, while no testing was done close to the baseline or week 3 biopsies. This may have influenced total RNA at post, as discussed above. Second, UBF and c-Myc protein were only measured at baseline and week 3, so it is unknown whether the changes persisted, and the 48 hour interval to the last session means a residual acute response cannot be excluded. Third, the RNA-seq data are of poly-A selected mRNA and cannot be used to assess rRNA, and the comparison with total RNA is therefore indirect. Fourth, total RNA is a proxy for ribosome content, and a noisy one: reported variation in total RNA change is large, and baseline total RNA has been found to correlate strongly and negatively with its own change [@godwin_2024; @lundberg_early_2020], which makes small differences between groups hard to interpret. Fifth, many of the contrasts were uncertain, with intervals including zero, and the volume effects in particular are best viewed as weak evidence for a direction. Finally, no dietary records were made, and the old control group was the only control group, so a time effect in the young cannot be assessed.

In conclusion, markers of ribosome biogenesis increased in both young and old participants, with a slower accumulation of total RNA in the old but no clear difference between age groups at post, and little influence of training volume. The transcriptional response was dominated by ECM remodelling and a down-regulation of RNA-processing genes, was largely age-independent, and was modified by training volume in the old only. Taken together, the data support a delayed rather than blunted ribosome biogenesis response in older adults.
